difficultyRationale: The pyramid's shape and its rationale are a well-known concept with a single defensible reading.
prompt: A team is deciding how to shape its automated test suite for a backend service. Which description best reflects the trade-off the test pyramid is meant to encode?
explanation: The pyramid is a shape, not a quota: many fast, cheap, isolated unit tests at the base; fewer, slower integration tests in the middle that check how components cooperate; and a small number of expensive, brittle end-to-end tests at the top that check the system as a whole. The shape follows from cost and fragility rising, and speed and precision of failure localization falling, as test scope grows.

options.text: Favor many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, and few slow, expensive end-to-end tests at the top.
options.explanation: This states the pyramid's actual rationale: it is a cost/speed/fragility trade-off, not an arbitrary ratio, and it explains why the base should dominate in count.

options.text: Invert the pyramid so most tests are end-to-end, since only end-to-end tests catch real bugs and unit tests are too narrow to be useful.
options.explanation: This describes the "ice-cream cone" anti-pattern the pyramid warns against: a suite dominated by slow, flaky end-to-end tests gives poor feedback speed and makes failures hard to localize, which is the opposite of what the pyramid recommends.

options.text: The pyramid says every layer should contain roughly the same number of tests, balancing speed and confidence evenly across unit, integration, and end-to-end levels.
options.explanation: An even split is not the pyramid's shape; the defining feature is a decreasing count as scope increases, driven by each higher layer being slower and more expensive to maintain per test.

options.text: The pyramid only concerns unit test line-coverage percentage, and integration or end-to-end tests fall outside the concept entirely.
options.explanation: The pyramid is explicitly about the relative proportion of tests across all three levels, not a coverage metric confined to one level.
